title: Friedberg numberings

based_on.title: Lecture notes in Computability Theory
based_on.pages: Version 2008-12-03; §33 Theorem 33.1, construction and verification, pp. 74–77; Definition 33.3 and Theorem 33.4, pp. 77–78; retiring-row containment repaired as in MILLER-CT-03

summary: List every computably enumerable set exactly once by retiring failed followers into distinct finite rows, then prove that standard indices cannot be translated computably into the unique row names.
abstract: Different programs can enumerate the same set, so the usual list of computably enumerable sets contains repetitions. Can one generate a list that contains every such set exactly once, while still recognizing membership in all its rows by one algorithm? Friedberg’s theorem answers yes. Temporary rows copy the standard enumerations, and failed rows are completed to distinct finite initial segments beginning at zero. The construction eventually preserves one row for each set with a missing number below one of its members; a separate computable list supplies the remaining finite initial segments, alongside the empty set and all natural numbers. The resulting family has unique names for all computably enumerable sets. Every new name can be compiled effectively into an ordinary program, but no terminating algorithm translates every ordinary program index into the unique name for its domain, since that would decide whether an arbitrary program has empty domain.
